_comment: Surgery pathway: thyroid swelling (goitre, nodule and carcinoma). Same architecture as pneumonia: shared core and surgery skills carry the examination method, this file adds thyroid-specific reasoning and overlays.
name: Thyroid swelling
fullName: Thyroid swelling: goitre, nodule and carcinoma
oneLine: A swelling in the front of the neck that moves on swallowing, and the decision of which ones to watch, cool down, resect or refer

chapters.title: Basics

chapters.blurb: Age, sex and district set the prior probability before the swelling is described
chapters.title: Patient particulars

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: In a thyroid swelling, age and sex carry unusual weight. Simple goitres gather in girls near puberty, nodular goitres in women in their twenties and thirties, and cancer spans the ages: papillary disease in the young, follicular disease in mid life, anaplastic disease in the old. A swelling in a man is less common and deserves the same careful workup, not reassurance.

chapters.blurb: Tempo in years, pain, pressure symptoms and function
chapters.title: History of presenting illness

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: A thyroid history reads in years, not days: a painless swelling noticed five or ten years ago, growing almost imperceptibly, is the classic benign tempo. Weeks of rapid growth, new hoarseness, or sudden painful enlargement after years of quiet are the tempo breaks that change the diagnosis.

skill.hx.surg.thyroid.expect: Expect a euthyroid patient with no functional symptoms in the common goitres. When toxicity is present on a longstanding nodular gland it is usually secondary, with cardiac symptoms leading, while a diffuse gland in a young patient with tremor, heat intolerance and eye symptoms points to primary toxicity.

chapters.blurb: Iodine, goitrogens, drugs, radiation and family
chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history

chapters.blurb: The toxic face, the pulse in sleep, the moist palm
chapters.title: General examination

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for the two opposite faces of thyroid function. The toxic patient is thin, restless and sweating, with an intent or staring expression; the hypothyroid patient is heavy and slow, with a puffy expressionless face, dry skin and thinning hair. Carcinoma declares itself late with pallor and weight loss.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Feel the pulse with function in mind. A fast regular pulse that stays fast even at rest fits primary toxicity; a fast irregular pulse in an older patient with a nodular gland suggests secondary toxicity with atrial fibrillation. A slow pulse with a heavy, cold-intolerant patient points the other way, toward hypothyroidism.

chapters.blurb: Inspection, palpation, movement on swallowing, nodes and bruit
chapters.title: Thyroid examination

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.expect: Watch the swelling as she swallows a sip of water. Upward movement on deglutition is the single sign that marks a swelling as thyroid, because the gland is fixed to the larynx. A gland that has lost this movement is fixed by invasion or inflammation, which is itself a finding.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.expect: Expect a multinodular gland to feel asymmetrical and bosselated with variable consistency, firmer where old bleeding has made a nodule tense. A stony hard fixed mass that will not move on swallowing, with absent carotid pulsation behind it, is carcinoma until proved otherwise.

skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.expect: Palpate the neck for nodes in every thyroid swelling, even when the gland itself feels benign. Papillary carcinoma spreads through lymph channels early, so enlarged nodes can be the presenting sign while the primary tumour is still small.

skill.reasoning.thyroid.basics.oneLine: Goitre means enlargement only; behaviour groups the causes

probes.a: Non-toxic goitre, toxic goitre, neoplastic disease and thyroiditis. Goitre alone says only that the gland is enlarged.
probes.q: Name the four behaviour groups of thyroid swellings.

probes.a: Because most nodules are benign and the task is to find the minority that are malignant, using function tests, ultrasound characterisation and needle sampling.
probes.q: Why does every thyroid nodule need risk stratification rather than direct surgery?

teach.heading: Goitre means enlargement, nothing more
teach.body:
The word goitre denotes any enlargement of the thyroid gland whatever its cause. It says nothing about function, nothing about benign or malignant, and nothing about treatment.

A thyroid swelling is recognised by position in the front of the neck, by shape, and above all by upward movement on swallowing, since the gland is fixed to the larynx. Loss of that movement means fixation by invasion or inflammation.

rows: Diffuse pubertal, colloid, multinodular, solitary nodule
Is it pressing on anything, and is it truly quiet in function
Diffuse Graves disease, toxic multinodular, toxic nodule

teach.heading: Four behaviour groups
Three questions that organise every case
points: Is the gland overactive, normally active or underactive in function?
Is the swelling diffuse or nodular, and does it fix to its surroundings or invade them?
Are there pressure effects on breathing, swallowing or voice, and are there nodes?

skill.reasoning.thyroid.basics.title: What a thyroid swelling is
skill.reasoning.thyroid.basics.why: Students drown in thyroid names because each swelling is taught as a separate disease. Grouping by behaviour first turns twenty names into four questions, and the right investigations then follow from the group rather than from memory.

skill.reasoning.thyroid.signs.oneLine: One gland read through consistency, fixity, nodes and function

probes.a: A benign multinodular gland is asymmetrical and bosselated with variable consistency and moves on swallowing, while carcinoma is stony hard, fixed, may not move on swallowing, and may show nodes, hoarseness or carotid encasement.
probes.q: Contrast the bedside findings of a benign nodular goitre with those of carcinoma.

probes.a: Tremor of the outstretched fingers and protruded tongue, a fast pulse that stays fast at rest, hot moist palms, and a systolic bruit over the upper poles of the gland from increased vascularity.
probes.q: Which bedside signs establish primary toxicity on examination?

sources.locator: The thyroid: physical signs of toxicity and malignancy
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.heading: Surface and consistency read the pathology
teach.body:
A diffuse hyperplastic gland feels smooth and uniformly firm. A multinodular gland feels asymmetrical and bosselated with consistency that varies from nodule to nodule, firmer where old bleeding has left a tense cyst.

A stony hard mass with an indistinct edge is carcinoma or Riedel thyroiditis until proved otherwise. A cyst that feels firm is not solid: fluid under tension inside a soft gland deceives the finger.

teach.heading: Fixity, nodes and nerve signs stage it
teach.body:
Test mobility in both planes and on swallowing. Fixity to strap muscles or trachea means infiltration, and a gland that will not move on deglutition has declared itself malignant or chronically inflamed.

Examine nodes in every case, since papillary cancer seeds them early. An encased carotid sheath with lost pulsation, Horner syndrome, or venous engorgement with raised arms all mark advanced or retrosternal disease.

rows: Painless early, painful when invading nerves

teach.heading: Benign against malignant at the bedside
Toxic signs and eye signs grade function
teach.body:
In primary toxicity look for fine tremor of outstretched fingers and the protruded tongue, hot moist palms felt just after the pulse, and a fast pulse that stays fast even at rest. A systolic bruit over the upper poles marks increased vascularity and comes late.

Separate lid retraction and lid lag from true exophthalmos, where sclera shows above and below the iris. Weak eye movements and conjunctival oedema belong to infiltrative eye disease and need eye protection.

skill.reasoning.thyroid.signs.title: The thyroid picture
skill.reasoning.thyroid.signs.why: No single thyroid sign is decisive, but consistency, fixity, nodes and function read together rarely lie. This synthesis is what turns a list of examination findings into a diagnosis and a plan.

skill.reasoning.thyroid.differential.oneLine: Goitres, cancers, thyroiditis and the non-thyroid mimics

probes.a: Thyroglossal cyst moves up when the tongue is protruded as well as on swallowing; a thyroid swelling moves only on swallowing.
probes.q: How do you separate a thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid swelling at the bedside?

probes.a: Painful tender gland with fever and raised ESR but low uptake in De Quervain thyroiditis; woody hard fixed gland mimicking cancer in Riedel thyroiditis; symmetrical rubbery gland with antibodies and eventual hypothyroidism in Hashimoto disease.
probes.q: How do the three chronic thyroiditis forms differ from carcinoma?

teach.heading: Nodular disease first

Years of growth, bosselated, variable firmness

teach.heading: Painful versus painless
teach.body:
Goitres and cancers start painless. Pain means bleeding into a nodule, acute suppurative infection after a sore throat, or De Quervain thyroiditis with fever and neck tenderness. Late cancer pain comes from nerve invasion, not from the tumour itself.

Hashimoto disease brings neck discomfort rather than true pain, with a rubbery symmetrical gland. Riedel disease is painless but woody hard and fixed, which is why it mimics cancer until sampled.

teach.heading: The non-thyroid mimics
points: Thyroglossal cyst: midline, moves on swallowing AND on tongue protrusion; a fistula near the hyoid follows an infected cyst.
Cervical nodes: multiple, do not move on swallowing unless fixed to the airway; tuberculous nodes carry weeks of history and characteristic skin changes.

Parathyroid and other neck lumps: a parathyroid adenoma or carcinoma can present as a palpable neck lump mimicking a lower-pole thyroid nodule, separated on ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging and confirmed by serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.
Retrosternal or aberrant thyroid tissue: suspected when no cervical gland explains the pressure signs, confirmed on scan.

skill.reasoning.thyroid.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of thyroid swelling
skill.reasoning.thyroid.differential.why: The front of the neck crowds thyroid, nodes, cysts and salivary tissue into a small space. A differential that moves from common goitres through cancers and thyroiditis to non-thyroid mimics stops the student anchoring on the first plausible name.

skill.investigation.thyroid.workup.oneLine: Function first, then map, then sample

probes.a: Serum TSH is the first-line test; a suppressed value points to an autonomous nodule and warrants a radionuclide scan, while sampling is directed at non-functioning nodules.
probes.q: What is the first blood test in a thyroid nodule, and what does a suppressed value change?

probes.a: Marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins and a taller-than-wide shape raise concern and guide which nodule to sample.
probes.q: Which ultrasound features raise concern for malignancy?

probes.a: Do not scan every enlarged gland; scan the solitary nodule, the suspected retrosternal goitre and ectopic tissue. A hot nodule rarely harbours cancer so aspiration targets cold nodules.
probes.q: When is a thyroid scan helpful, and when is it not?

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: TSH first, always
teach.body:
Begin every nodule workup with serum TSH with free hormones. A suppressed value points to an autonomously functioning nodule, which is usually benign and warrants a radionuclide scan rather than direct sampling.

Never proceed to biopsy before checking TSH: sampling a hot nodule misses the diagnosis and wastes the procedure. TSH also sets the baseline for follow-up after any treatment.

teach.heading: Ultrasound maps, scan sorts function, needle decides

rows: TSH with free T4 and T3
Nodule character, nodes, which to sample
CT or MRI without iodinated contrast
Compressive symptoms or impalpable lower border

teach.heading: What not to order first
teach.body:
Do not scan all enlarged glands: scanning helps the solitary nodule, the suspected retrosternal goitre and ectopic tissue, and little else. Ultrasound separates solid from cystic and finds impalpable nodules, but alone it cannot diagnose cancer.

Avoid iodinated contrast studies where an autonomous nodule could be tipped into toxicity, and never delay referral for suspected cancer while waiting for a low-yield test. Plain neck radiography is outdated for assessing retrosternal extension; cross-sectional imaging without iodinated contrast and direct vocal cord assessment guide compressive or retrosternal disease.

skill.investigation.thyroid.workup.title: Investigating the thyroid swelling
skill.investigation.thyroid.workup.why: Thyroid investigations have a strict order, and each test answers a different question. Function first avoids sampling a hot nodule; mapping next aims the needle; the needle result then directs management.

skill.reasoning.thyroid.diagnosis.oneLine: Function by anatomy by behaviour: the complete diagnosis

probes.a: A hot functioning nodule on scanning rarely harbours malignancy, so aspiration is directed at non-functioning nodules after TSH and scan have sorted function.
probes.q: Why does a hot nodule usually escape needle sampling?

probes.a: Benign cytology means clinical and ultrasound surveillance; malignant or suspicious cytology means referral for diagnostic lobectomy or thyroidectomy through a multidisciplinary team; indeterminate cytology uses repeat sampling or diagnostic lobectomy, with molecular testing where available to refine risk.
probes.q: How does the cytology result decide the next step?

sources.locator: The thyroid gland: diagnosis of nodules and cancer
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Three axes make the diagnosis
teach.body:
A complete thyroid diagnosis states function, anatomy and behaviour together. Function: toxic, euthyroid or hypothyroid from TSH and clinical signs. Anatomy: diffuse or nodular, solitary or multinodular, with retrosternal extension stated or excluded.

Behaviour: benign, suspicious or malignant from cytology and red flags. Any statement missing one axis is incomplete: a multinodular goitre is not a diagnosis until its function and its cytology are attached.

teach.heading: Reading the cytology result
teach.body:
Fine needle sampling reports in standardised categories that guide management. Benign means surveillance, not surgery. Malignant or suspicious means surgical referral, usually diagnostic lobectomy or thyroidectomy decided with the multidisciplinary team.

Indeterminate results warrant repeat ultrasound-guided sampling or diagnostic lobectomy; molecular testing refines risk where available, but in India is largely confined to specialised referral centres. A non-diagnostic sample is never reassuring: repeat it rather than discharging the patient on its strength.

teach.heading: Red flags that upgrade any diagnosis
points: Rapidly enlarging, hard or fixed nodule with lost movement on swallowing.
New hoarseness, vocal cord palsy, stridor or dysphagia from invasion.
Hard cervical nodes, especially with a small or impalpable primary.
Childhood neck irradiation or family history of thyroid cancer.
Compressive symptoms or engorged chest veins suggesting retrosternal growth.

skill.reasoning.thyroid.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis of thyroid swelling
skill.reasoning.thyroid.diagnosis.why: A thyroid diagnosis is a composite, not a single word, and the cytology category plus red flags decide whether the patient is watched, cooled down or referred for surgery. Getting this synthesis exact is what keeps benign disease out of the operating theatre and cancer out of follow-up.

skill.treatment.thyroid.management.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of modality and principle: which nodules are watched, which are cooled to normal function first, and which go to the operating theatre or the cancer team. Specific agents, activities and durations come from your current national or institutional guideline at the time of treatment. CliniX does not prescribe.
skill.treatment.thyroid.management.oneLine: Watch the benign, cool the toxic, resect the malignant or compressing

probes.a: Cytologically benign nodules are managed with clinical and ultrasound surveillance rather than intervention, with defined referral thresholds for growth, new symptoms or functional change.
probes.q: How is a cytologically benign nodule managed?

probes.a: Render the patient euthyroid with an antithyroid drug first, control adrenergic symptoms, then offer definitive radioiodine or surgery, with surgery preferred for large, retrosternal or compressing glands.
probes.q: What is the sequence of treating a toxic nodular goitre?

probes.a: Suspected cancer goes to a thyroid multidisciplinary team for surgery, usually lobectomy or thyroidectomy with compartment dissection for proven nodes, then hormone replacement with suppression, selective radioiodine ablation and thyroglobulin plus ultrasound surveillance.
probes.q: Outline the management of confirmed differentiated thyroid cancer.

sources.locator: The thyroid gland: treatment of goitre and cancer
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Benign and euthyroid: watch, do not cut
teach.body:
Nodules with benign cytology need clinical and ultrasound surveillance, not intervention. Re-examine the neck, repeat function tests and rescan at planned intervals, and sample again if a nodule grows or changes character.

Counsel the household on iodised salt where deficiency is endemic. Reassure without discharging: give explicit return thresholds of rapid growth, new hoarseness, breathing or swallowing difficulty, or neck nodes.

teach.heading: Toxic: cool down first, then definitive treatment
teach.body:
A toxic nodular gland is rendered euthyroid with an antithyroid drug before any definitive step, while adrenergic symptoms are controlled and the heart is protected. Operating or ablating through uncontrolled toxicity is never the plan.

Definitive treatment is radioiodine or surgery. Surgery is preferred for large, retrosternal or compressing glands, for suspected cancer alongside toxicity, and where eye disease or patient choice argues against radioiodine. Lifelong hormone replacement follows total removal.

teach.heading: Malignant or suspicious: the cancer team operates
teach.body:
Nodules with malignant or suspicious cytology are referred to a thyroid multidisciplinary team. Surgery is the mainstay: lobectomy for low-risk contained tumours (unifocal, intrathyroidal, under 4 cm, no nodal spread), whereas total thyroidectomy with central compartment dissection is indicated for larger tumours, gross extrathyroidal extension, or proven nodal metastasis.

After total removal, levothyroxine replacement with TSH suppression is tailored to recurrence risk. Radioactive iodine ablation is reserved for intermediate- or high-risk disease (extrathyroidal invasion, nodal or distant spread), while low-risk resected disease is spared ablation. Surveillance relies on neck ultrasound and serum thyroglobulin; medullary cancer adds calcitonin and family screening.

teach.heading: Compression and the Indian referral map
teach.body:
Large or compressive nodules with local symptoms need surgery for the pressure itself, whatever the cytology. Assess the airway and vocal cords before operating on retrosternal or longstanding giant goitres.

In Indian practice, TSH, neck ultrasound and needle sampling are available at most district hospitals, while scanning, endocrine surgery and cancer teams sit at medical colleges and higher centres. Refer promptly for hard fixed swellings, hoarseness, nodes, stridor, rapid growth or suppressed TSH with toxicity.

skill.treatment.thyroid.management.title: Managing thyroid swelling
skill.treatment.thyroid.management.why: Thyroid management is allocation, not prescription: most nodules are watched, toxic glands are cooled before definitive treatment, and cancers move as a team decision to surgery with planned follow-up. Knowing which track the patient belongs on matters more than any single drug name.

diagnosis.answer: Multinodular goitre, clinically euthyroid, with benign cytology on needle sampling.

differentialModel.answer: Multinodular goitre, euthyroid. Consider a dominant adenoma, early papillary or follicular carcinoma, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and a toxic nodule if function changes.

skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.finding: No palpable cervical lymph nodes in any group. No supraclavicular fullness.

skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.finding: Swelling moves freely upward on swallowing a sip of water. No upward movement on protrusion of the tongue.

skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.finding: Fingers get below both lower poles on swallowing. No venous engorgement over the upper chest. No facial congestion on raising both arms overhead.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.finding: No bruit over either lobe. No thrill on palpation.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.finding: No lid retraction, no lid lag, no exophthalmos. Eye movements full. No conjunctival oedema.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.finding: Asymmetrical bosselated swelling over the front of the lower neck, right lobe more prominent, about the size of a small lime on the right. Skin over it normal. Swelling rises on swallowing.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.finding: Both lobes and isthmus enlarged, surface bosselated with several firm nodules of varying size. No stony hard area. Gland mobile sideways and moves freely on swallowing. Trachea central. Carotid pulsations felt behind both lobes.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Comfortable middle-aged woman, average build, no weight loss. Calm, no restlessness or sweating. No pallor or puffiness of the face.

skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.finding: No tremor of outstretched fingers or tongue. Palms dry and warm, not moist. Pulse regular, no hypertension.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Temperature 36.8 C. Pulse 78 per minute regular. Blood pressure 124/80. Respiratory rate 16 per minute. SpO2 98 percent on room air.

cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

breathing.reply: No difficulty in breathing, doctor. I sleep flat on my back without any trouble, and there is no whistling sound.

comorbidity.reply: No diabetes, no blood pressure problem. I have never been admitted to hospital before this.

diet_iodine.reply: We use loose salt from the market, not the packed kind. We eat cabbage and turnip often in winter since they grow nearby.

eye_symptoms.reply: No, my eyes are as before. No staring, no difficulty in closing the lids, no double vision.

family.reply: My mother also had a swelling in the neck in her old age, but she never took treatment for it. My two sisters are fine so far.

heat_weight.reply: My weight is steady and I eat as usual. I do not feel extra hot, and I do not sweat more than others at home.

medications.reply: No regular medicines. A local practitioner once gave me some tablets for a month but the swelling stayed the same, so I stopped.

menstrual.reply: My monthly cycles are regular and as before, nothing changed.

onset_course.reply: I first noticed it about six years ago, a small fullness in front of the neck. It has grown very slowly since then, without any sudden increase.

pain.reply: No pain at all, doctor. It has never hurt, not even when I press it.

palpitation_tremor.reply: No racing of the heart, no shaking of the hands. I sleep well at night, seven hours easily.

presenting.reply: Doctor, I have this swelling in the front of my neck since many years. It is slowly getting bigger and now it shows, so my family asked me to come.

radiation.reply: No, I never had any radiation or special treatment to the neck as a child.

residence.reply: We live in a hill village in Tehri Garhwal. I was born there and have lived there all my life. Many women in our village have such neck swellings.

swallowing.reply: I swallow food and water normally. Sometimes I feel a heaviness but nothing gets stuck.

voice.reply: My voice is as always. No hoarseness, no change while speaking.

calcitonin.label: Serum calcitonin
calcitonin.note: Not indicated here: no diarrhoea, no family tumours, no medullary features. It is reserved for suspected medullary disease.

fnac.label: Ultrasound guided FNAC of dominant nodule
fnac.note: The key test: benign cytology moves her to surveillance, while suspicious cytology would move her to the surgical team.
fnac.result: Benign colloid nodule with cystic change. No malignant cells. Standardised category consistent with benign disease.

scan.label: Radionuclide thyroid scan
scan.note: Not indicated: her TSH is normal, and scanning every enlarged gland adds nothing. Scanning is reserved for suppressed TSH or suspected retrosternal tissue.

tsh.label: Serum TSH with free T4
tsh.note: The first test in every nodule: normal function here means no scan and no cooling treatment, only structural workup.
tsh.result: TSH normal. Free T4 within normal limits. Clinically and biochemically euthyroid.

usg.label: Neck ultrasound
usg.note: Mapping aims the needle at the right nodule and records nodes. No suspicious nodes here, which supports the benign course.
usg.result: Both lobes enlarged with multiple nodules, largest on the right. No marked hypoechogenicity, no microcalcifications, no irregular margins. No suspicious cervical nodes.

xray_neck.label: Neck X-ray for trachea
xray_neck.note: Not indicated: plain neck radiography is outdated for assessing airway or retrosternal extension. Palpating below both lower poles and a central trachea already exclude retrosternal extension at the bedside; cross-sectional imaging without iodinated contrast is reserved for when the lower border cannot be reached or compression occurs.

managementModel.answer: Clinical and ultrasound surveillance with repeat function tests, household iodised salt counselling, explicit return thresholds for growth, hoarseness, pressure symptoms or nodes, and surgical referral if cytology, function or compression change.

cases.opening: Meena Devi, 44, has come to the surgery outpatient clinic with her daughter. A bosselated swelling fills the front of her lower neck. Introduce yourself and take a history.

patient.name: Meena Devi
patient.residence: Rural hill village, Tehri Garhwal, lives with husband and two children

teachingPoints: The tempo does the first half of the diagnosis: six years of painless slow growth with preserved movement on swallowing is the classic benign multinodular course.
Endemic context matters: lifelong residence in a sub Himalayan village with affected relatives and non iodised loose salt explains a simple multinodular goitre far better than a tumour.
Movement on swallowing marks the swelling as thyroid, while absent tongue-protrusion movement excludes a thyroglossal cyst without any test.

Fingers getting below both lower poles with a central trachea excludes retrosternal extension at the bedside, so routine imaging for retrosternal disease is unnecessary; plain neck radiography is outdated, and contrast-sparing CT or MRI is reserved for when the lower border cannot be reached or compression occurs.
TSH first, then mapping, then sampling: normal function meant no scan and no antithyroid treatment, and benign cytology means surveillance with thresholds, not surgery.
A solitary-feeling dominant nodule in a multinodular gland is common: about half of solitary presenters actually carry several nodules, so the whole gland is mapped, not just the lump.
cases.title: A hill woman with six years of neck swelling
